title_en: Several Provisions (II) of the Supreme People's Court on Issues concerning the Specific Application of Law in the Trial of Disputes over Infringement of New Plant Variety Rights

articles.content_en:
Where co-owners of a right to a new plant variety (hereinafter referred to as the “variety right”) or of the right to apply for a new plant variety have an agreement on the exercise of the right, the People's Court shall handle the matter in accordance with the agreement. Where there is no agreement or the agreement is unclear, and a co-owner claims that he or she may independently implement the right or license others to implement it by way of an ordinary license, the People's Court shall uphold the claim.
Where a co-owner independently implements the variety right, and other co-owners claim that the benefits from such implementation shall be distributed among the co-owners, the People's Court shall not uphold the claim, unless the other co-owners have evidence proving that they lack the capacity or conditions for implementation.
Where one of the co-owners licenses another person to implement the variety right, and other co-owners claim that the license fees collected shall be distributed among the co-owners, the People's Court shall uphold the claim.

Where the transfer of a variety right has not been registered and publicly announced by the competent administrative departments of agriculture and forestry under the State Council, and the transferee initiates an action for infringement of the variety right in the name of the variety right holder, the People's Court shall not accept the case.

Reproductive material protected by a variety right shall have reproductive capacity, and the new individuals produced by reproduction shall be identical to the authorized variety in characteristics and traits.
The reproductive material mentioned in the preceding paragraph is not limited to reproductive material obtained through the reproduction method described in the variety right application documents.

Where an intention to sell reproductive material of an authorized variety is expressed by means of advertising, exhibition, or other means, the People's Court may determine and handle it as a sales act.

Where a person plants reproductive material of an authorized variety, the People's Court may, based on the specific circumstances of the case, determine and handle it as an act of production or reproduction.

Where the variety right holder or an interested party (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “right holder”) adduces evidence proving that the name used for the reproductive material of the allegedly infringing variety is the same as the name of the authorized variety, the People's Court may presume that the reproductive material of the allegedly infringing variety is reproductive material of the authorized variety; where there is evidence proving that it is not reproductive material of the authorized variety, the People's Court may determine that the alleged infringer constitutes an act of counterfeiting a variety, and shall determine civil liability by reference to the relevant provisions on counterfeiting registered trademarks.

Where the entrusted party or licensee produces or reproduces reproductive material of an authorized variety beyond the scale or region agreed upon with the variety right holder, or sells reproductive material of an authorized variety beyond the scale agreed upon with the variety right holder, and the variety right holder requests a judgment ordering the entrusted party or licensee to bear infringement liability, the People's Court shall uphold the claim according to law.

Where the alleged infringer knows or should know that another person is committing an act infringing a variety right, yet still provides services such as purchase, storage, transportation, or processing for the purpose of reproduction, or provides conditions such as relevant evidentiary materials, the People's Court may, pursuant to Article 1169 of the Civil Code, determine that the alleged infringer is aiding another person in committing a tortious act.

Where the alleged infringing object can be used both as reproductive material and as harvested material, and the alleged infringer claims that the alleged infringing object is used as harvested material for consumption rather than for production or reproduction, the alleged infringer shall bear the corresponding burden of adducing evidence.

Where a farmer, within the scope of land agreed upon in his or her household rural land contract management contract, self-propagates and self-uses reproductive material of an authorized variety, and the right holder claims that this constitutes infringement, the People's Court shall not uphold the claim.
With respect to acts other than those provided for in the preceding paragraph, where the alleged infringer claims that the act constitutes a farmer's self-propagation and self-use of reproductive material of an authorized variety as provided for in the Seed Law, the People's Court shall determine the matter by comprehensively considering factors such as the purpose, scale, and whether the act is for profit.

Where a seller sells reproductive material of an allegedly infringing variety without knowing and without a duty to know that it was sold without the permission of the variety right holder, and adduces evidence proving that it has a lawful source, the People's Court may not order the seller to bear compensation liability, but shall order the seller to cease the sale and bear the reasonable expenses paid by the right holder to stop the infringing act.
For the lawful source mentioned in the preceding paragraph, the seller shall generally adduce evidence proving that the purchase channel is lawful, the price is reasonable, there is an actual specific supplier, and the sales act complies with the relevant production and operation licensing system, among others.

Where the People's Court determines that the infringing act is established based on the facts of infringement of a variety right that have been ascertained, it may first render a judgment ordering cessation of the infringement, and may, pursuant to the party's request and the specific circumstances of the case, order measures to be taken to prevent the spread and reproduction of the alleged infringing object, such as deactivation.

Where, for the purpose of determining the amount of damages, the right holder has made best efforts to adduce evidence, and the books and materials related to the infringing act are mainly in the possession of the alleged infringer, the People's Court may order the alleged infringer to provide the books and materials related to the infringing act; if the alleged infringer fails to provide them or provides false books or materials, the People's Court may determine the amount of damages by reference to the right holder's claims and the evidence provided.

Where the alleged infringer engages in acts that obstruct the adducing of evidence, such as resisting preservation or arbitrarily unsealing, transferring, or damaging the preserved property, rendering it impossible to ascertain the relevant facts of the case, the People's Court may presume that the right holder's claim regarding the matters to be proved by such evidence is established. Where the circumstances provided for in Article 111 of the Civil Procedure Law are constituted, legal liability shall be pursued according to law.

Where a variety right is restored according to law after its termination, and the right holder requests the unit or individual that implemented the variety right to pay fees for implementing the variety right during the termination period, the People's Court may reasonably determine the fees by reference to the relevant license fees for implementing the variety right, taking into account factors such as the type of variety, planting time, scale of operation, and market value at the time.

Where, without permission, from the date of announcement of passing the preliminary examination of a variety right to the date of grant of the variety right, another person produces, reproduces, or sells the reproductive material of the authorized variety, or, for commercial purposes, repeatedly uses the reproductive material of the authorized variety in producing the reproductive material of another variety, and the right holder claims compensation for loss of benefits with respect thereto, the People's Court may handle the matter as a dispute over the use fee for the period of temporary protection, and may reasonably determine the amount of such use fee by reference to the relevant license fees for implementing the variety right, taking into account factors such as the type of variety, planting time, scale of operation, and market value at the time.
Where the alleged infringing act provided for in the preceding paragraph continues to after the grant of the variety right, and the right holder claims both the use fee for the period of temporary protection of the variety right and damages for infringement, the People's Court may consolidate the hearing, but shall calculate and handle them separately.

Where a specialized issue involved in a case of dispute over infringement of a variety right requires expert evaluation, the parties shall, through consultation, select an expert from the list of experts in the relevant field or from the experts recommended by the competent administrative departments of agriculture and forestry under the State Council to the People's Court; if consultation fails, the People's Court shall designate an expert therefrom.

For varieties for which there is no molecular marker detection method, such as gene fingerprint profiling, for expert evaluation, industry-common methods may be used to judge the identity of the characteristics and traits between the authorized variety and the alleged infringing object.

Where a party that disagrees with the expert opinion applies to the People's Court for re-examination, supplementary expert evaluation, or re-evaluation, but fails to provide reasonable grounds and evidence, the People's Court shall not grant the application.

Where expert evaluation is carried out by molecular marker detection methods such as gene fingerprint profiling, and the number of differential loci between the sample to be tested and the control sample is less than but close to the critical value, the alleged infringer claiming that the characteristics and traits of the two are different shall bear the burden of adducing evidence; the People's Court may also, upon a party's application, adopt methods such as expanding the detected loci for additional testing or extracting a standard sample of the authorized variety for testing, and make a determination in light of other relevant factors.

Where the conclusion of field observation testing differs from the conclusion of molecular marker detection such as gene fingerprint profiling, the People's Court shall take the conclusion of field observation testing as the prevailing conclusion.

These Provisions shall come into force on July 7, 2021. Where the relevant judicial interpretations previously issued by this Court are inconsistent with these Provisions, these Provisions shall prevail.
